question: Police searches of media outlets: the case of Il Corriere Fiorentino

On 31 July, Italian police searched both the offices of Il Corriere Fiorentino and the home of one of its journalists, Simone Innocenti, on suspicion of conspiring with one or more public officials to disclose and use official secrets.

The raid was requested by the Florence Public Prosecutor’s Office as part of an investigation concerning a 17 May Corriere article on the 22 April suicide of a 25-year-old female cadet who was enrolled in the Carabinieri’s Academy for Warrant Officers and Sergeants in Florence.

These raids are clearly at odds not only with the case-law of the European Court of Human Rights and of the Italian Constitutional Court – which have long upheld the confidentiality of journalistic sources – but also with the new rules laid down by the EU’s Media Freedom Act, in particular Article 4(3)(b) thereof. In the light of its recent recommendations on the state of press freedom in Italy: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this state of affairs?

If so, what measures will it take to penalise the above acts, which constitute a clear infringement of two principles guaranteed by the European Union, namely freedom of the press and freedom of information?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.10.2024) Safeguarding media freedom and pluralism has been at the heart of the Commission’s efforts to uphold democracy and the rule of law in the EU.

Article 4(3) of the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA)1 requires Member States to effectively protect journalistic sources and confidential communications and to refrain from taking certain measures, including subjecting journalists’ corporate or private premises to search for the purpose of obtaining information related to or capable of identifying journalistic sources or confidential communication.
Nonetheless, Article 4(4) of the EMFA provides for a derogation allowing Member States to take such measures under certain strict conditions.

These conditions include the requirement that the possibility to take the measure is provided for by EU or national law, that the measure is justified by an overriding reason of public interest and is proportionate, and that the measure is subject to prior authorisation by a judicial authority or an independent and impartial decision-making authority or, in duly justified exceptional and urgent cases, is subsequently authorised by such an authority without undue delay.
These EMFA provisions shall apply from 8 August 2025. As part of its annual Rule of Law Report, the Commission assesses the situation on media freedom and pluralism in all Member States2.

The chapter on Italy notes that in spite of targeted rules on the protection of journalists, the situation regarding their safety and working conditions as well as the increasing prevalence of strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs) cases3 remain an issue4. If they consider that national measures infringe their rights, citizens and businesses can resort to the competent national authorities.
